Source title: Qakbot Malware Disrupted in International Cyber Takedown
Publisher: U.S. Attorney's Office, Central District of California (U.S. Department of Justice)
Key fact (own words): The DOJ says the FBI gained access to Qakbot's infrastructure, identified over 700,000 infected computers worldwide (more than 200,000 in the US), and redirected botnet traffic through FBI-controlled servers so that infected machines downloaded a file that uninstalled the malware.
Notes: DOJ says Qakbot mainly spread through spam emails with malicious attachments or links and was used to deliver ransomware. Countries listed took part in the operation, not necessarily where victims were. Figures are the authorities' own claims. DOJ says the action did not remove other malware already on victim computers.

Source title: Qakbot-affiliated actors distribute Ransom Knight malware despite infrastructure takedown
Key fact (own words): Talos says a phishing campaign delivering Ransom Knight ransomware and the Remcos backdoor began before the takedown and continued after it, and assesses with moderate confidence that Qakbot affiliates are behind it, based on matching LNK file metadata.
Notes: Talos had not seen Qakbot itself distributed after the takedown. Its view that only C2 servers were hit is a hedged inference, not a confirmed fact.

Source title: Hibernating Qakbot: A Comprehensive Study and In-depth Campaign Analysis
Publisher: Zscaler ThreatLabz (authors: Meghraj Nandanwar, Satyam Singh, Pradeep Mahato)
Key fact (own words): Zscaler ThreatLabz reports a significant drop in Qakbot activity after June 2023, which it says may point to a temporary pause by the operators, but it states the reasons are unclear.
Notes: The study says the cause is unclear. It was published before the takedown. The monthly table covers only January to May, and the source reflects Zscaler's own telemetry.

Source title: Microsoft Threat Intelligence posts on new Qakbot phishing campaign
Date published: 2023-12-16 (as displayed in my browser; SC Media reports Dec 15)
Key fact (own words): Microsoft Threat Intelligence reported on December 16, 2023 a low-volume Qakbot phishing campaign that began on December 11, aimed at the hospitality industry, using an email with a PDF attachment containing a link that downloaded a signed installer file, which then launched Qakbot.
Notes: 'Low volume' has no figures behind it. Microsoft does not say these are the same operators as before the takedown. This is one vendor's own telemetry. The date difference with SC Media is probably a time-zone effect, not confirmed.

Source title: New QakBot phishing campaign appears, months after FBI takedown
Publisher: SC Media / SC World (author: Simon Hendery)
Key fact (own words): SC Media reports that Microsoft's Threat Intelligence team announced a new Qakbot phishing campaign a few months after the law enforcement takedown, and links it back to Cisco Talos's earlier finding about the same group.
Notes: Adds no new evidence, because it relays Microsoft's X post (S04) and Talos (S02). Not counted as independent confirmation. States Microsoft's post as Dec. 15. Quotes another researcher's X opinion that the new version resembles the old one; unverified.

Key fact (own words): MITRE ATT&CK lists QakBot as software S0650, describing it as a banking trojan used mainly by financially motivated actors that grew into a delivery tool for ransomware, and it catalogues the techniques the malware is known to use.
Notes: Reference for technique names and IDs only. Not evidence of what happened in the campaigns studied. A technique is mapped only when one of S01 to S04 supports it.
